name: Namibia
summary: German South West Africa (1884–1915), then ruled by South Africa; independent in 1990 after a long liberation war.

knownFor.label: Namib Desert dunes
knownFor.note: Some of the tallest sand dunes.

knownFor.label: Herero and Nama genocide
knownFor.note: German colonial killings (1904–08); Germany recognised them as genocide in 2021.

location.value: South-west Africa on the Atlantic; 825,615 km².

terrain.value: Namib and Kalahari deserts, central plateau.

climate.value: Mostly hot and dry: the Namib coast is cool and foggy with almost no rain, while the north-east gets summer rain.

resources.value: Diamonds, many mined from the seabed, uranium (Rössing and Husab mines), zinc and copper, fish in the cold Benguela Current, and wildlife.

disasters.value: Repeated droughts, such as in 2013 and 2019, plus floods in the northern Cuvelai basin.

population.value: 3,022,401 (2023 census, per the text; the infobox labels the same count as 2025).

urbanisation.value: About half the people live in towns; Windhoek, the capital, is by far the largest city, followed by towns such as Rundu and Walvis Bay.

disease.value: High HIV rates, though treatment has greatly reduced deaths since the 2000s; malaria in the north, and tuberculosis.

migration.value: About 40,000 exiles returned in 1989–90 under UN supervision; since then many people have moved from the rural north to towns.

economicBase.value: Mining supplies about 25% of revenue (18.0% of GDP in Q3 2023) and Namibia is a major source of gem-quality diamonds; uranium output was 750 tons a year in 2019; tourism is 14.5% of GDP. Fishing is not covered by the part of the page read.

tradeRoutes.value: Walvis Bay, the main port, and the Trans-Kalahari and Trans-Caprivi highways linking it to Botswana, Zambia and South Africa.

wealth.value: An upper-middle-income country by World Bank measures, but wealth is very unevenly spread.

moneyAndTax.value: The Namibian dollar, introduced in 1993 and tied one-to-one to the South African rand, which also circulates.

inequality.value: Income disparity is among the highest in the world: Gini 59.1 (2015).

governmentType.value: A unitary semi-presidential democratic republic; the constitution was adopted on 9 February 1990.

keyRulers.value: Sam Nujoma (first president, 15 years from 1990) and Hage Geingob (elected 2014, died 4 February 2024). Later and present leaders are not named here.

succession.value: Presidents are elected every five years, limited to two terms; power has passed peacefully between presidents since 1990.

institutions.value: The National Assembly, National Council, an independent judiciary and an Ombudsman, set up by the 1990 constitution.

stability.value: Peaceful and democratic since 1990, apart from a short-lived separatist attack in the Caprivi Strip in 1999.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: The Namibian Defence Force, formed in 1990 by merging former SWAPO guerrillas and South West African forces.

majorWars.value: The Namibian War of Independence (1966–90), fought by SWAPO’s armed wing against South African rule, mostly in the north and from Angola.

territoryChange.value: Walvis Bay, annexed by the Cape Colony in 1878, was ceded to Namibia by South Africa in 1994.

alliancesRivals.value: Member of SADC, the Southern African Customs Union, the African Union and the Commonwealth; close ties with Angola and South Africa.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: The University of Namibia (1992) and the Namibia University of Science and Technology; adult literacy has risen to about 90%.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Long paved roads, the TransNamib railway inland from Walvis Bay and Lüderitz, and Hosea Kutako airport near Windhoek.

religion.value: 2023: Christian 87.9% (Lutheran 43.7%, Catholic 22.8%, Anglican 17.0%), other religions 10.5%, no religion 1.6%.

languageWriting.value: English is the official language; Oshiwambo is the most widely spoken, with Afrikaans, Otjiherero, Nama/Damara, German and others.

artsArchitecture.value: German colonial buildings such as Windhoek’s Christuskirche, ancient rock art at Twyfelfontein, and Herero women’s dress.

socialStructure.value: Ovambo majority; Herero, Nama, San and others.

sharedIdentity.value: A national identity built around “One Namibia, One Nation” after 1990, alongside strong ethnic and regional identities.

dailyLife.value: In the north many families live in homesteads growing mahangu (pearl millet); porridge with meat, often grilled at a braai, is common.

neighbours.value: Angola and Zambia to the north, Botswana to the east, and South Africa to the south and south-east.

ideasReligions.value: A policy of national reconciliation after independence, and talks with Germany over the Herero and Nama genocide of 1904–08.

colonisation.value: A German colony from 1884 (German troops killed about 65,000 Herero and 10,000 Nama in 1904–08); a South African mandate from 1920; independent on 21 March 1990.

riseSignals.value: Independence from South Africa on 21 March 1990.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; its peaceful transition to independence in 1990 is often seen as a success.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Still an independent republic; it took over Walvis Bay from South Africa in 1994.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
